content:
If it seems like our president is auditioning for a job at HGTV, you’re not imagining things.

For the first time since the nationwide ground stop on Friday, President Donald Trump spoke to reporters on Monday and immediately called one a “loser” for not acknowledging White House renovations.

NBC News White House correspondent Yamiche Alcindor asked the president to respond to criticism that he was “too focused on D.C. construction projects” instead of the airline industry.

“Well, if you take a look at the White House, it’s flawless,” Trump said, later telling Alcindor, “This doesn’t cost money. This is peanuts. And I pay for it. ... This is called talent. Talent. You don’t have talent.”

“Losers like you come out, and they say, ‘Why are you focused on the White House?’” Trump continued. “Because the White House is the symbol of our country.”

Trump pointed to the White House and said, “The White House should look like that.” He then pointed at a nearby stone and said, “And the stone should look like this. Look at this stone.”

Alcindor posted on X that Trump’s answer to her was “doubling down” on these construction projects, which have been part of Trump’s priority since returning to office.

HuffPost reached out to Alcindor for further comment.

“President Trump’s commitment to restoring our Nation’s treasured landmarks should be celebrated,” Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, told HuffPost in a statement.

Last year, Trump took down the East Wing of the White House to make space for his idealized ballroom; over the summer, he tried to renovate the Reflecting Pool, paved over the White House Rose Garden and gave the Oval Office a maximalist makeover to the point where former President Barack Obama jokingly compared it to Saddam Hussein remodeling the Cheesecake Factory.

Currently, Trump is fighting for a 250-foot triumphal arch between the Lincoln Memorial and the Arlington National Cemetery, which he recast as a military tribute.

To political observers, pivoting from an aviation crisis to a lecture on stonework might seem like a simple deflection because the president didn’t have an answer. But psychologists who study ego and status told HuffPost that Trump’s fixation on physical monuments serves a very specific psychological purpose.

“Physical projects offer a stage for grand displays — pomp and circumstance,” Craig Malkin, a psychologist and Harvard Medical School lecturer, told HuffPost. “You can point to a building, photograph it and wrap yourself in its grandeur. For someone who constantly needs to shore up a sense of greatness, legislative work demands tedious negotiation and shared credit, with little opportunity for immediate personal glory.”

In Malkin’s book, “Rethinking Narcissism,” he describes that when some people depend heavily on feeling exceptional, any questions or uncertainty can make them feel worthless. By attacking Alcindor and turning his answer into “self-congratulation” over renovating the White House, Trump elevates criticism into a sales pitch for what he considers his strength.

“He turns a challenge to his leadership into a story about other people’s failure to recognize his greatness,” Malkin said. “That obsession [with exceptionalism] hijacks the conversation, fueling startling non sequiturs and insults.”

John Gartner, a psychologist and former assistant professor at Johns Hopkins University Medical School, noted that pivoting back to construction also serves as a psychological retreat into familiar, low-stress territory. (Did we forget the president worked in real estate before politics?)

“He reverts back to things he feels comfortable with, that he’s excited about, that matter to him,” Gartner told HuffPost. “He’s playing with his Legos and building monuments to himself.”

Gartner described Trump’s fixation on monuments as classic “self-aggrandizement.” “When you look at leaders throughout history who build monuments to themselves, it’s indicative of pathological narcissism,” he said.

Trump bringing up his fixation in response to a question about a nationwide situation is also significant, according to Sheldon Solomon, a social psychologist known for co-developing terror management theory. Solomon compared Trump’s response to Alcindor’s question to the saying, “Nero fiddled while Rome burned.” While Emperor Nero did not literally play the fiddle when Rome burned down, the idiom refers to a person in power ignoring catastrophes affecting others and focusing on their own personal enjoyment.

“Having his name on buildings and arches and airports and rivers [is] much more important to maintain and magnify his ego — nothing else matters,” Solomon told HuffPost. “When psychological shit hits the proverbial fan, he regresses back to his long-standing efforts to surround himself with golden buildings in pursuit of fame, fortune and (ultimately) immortality.”

While Trump may still be pressed on legislation and crisis management, the president appears determined to ensure his legacy is measured in physical things that are much harder to undo — and much easier to point at.
